paras: This summary covers a grievance filed on 12 May concerning the communication of a change to the night shift pattern at one site. It is written for the two parties and for the executive team, and it separates what was alleged, what was reported second hand, and what the investigation concluded. Those three are kept in separate paragraphs on purpose.

The allegations were three. First, that the change to the shift pattern was never communicated to the affected employees. Second, that a request to review it was raised twice with the plant manager and not escalated. Third, that one employee was told her hours would return to normal in June and they did not.

What was reported at second hand. Two colleagues told the investigator that they had heard the change discussed in a corridor conversation in April. Neither was present at any meeting where it was decided, and neither could give a date. This is recorded here because it was said, and it is labelled as hearsay because it cannot be substantiated. It does not form part of the findings.

Findings. The first allegation is substantiated: the change exists in the radio log of 3 May and in no written communication to employees. The second is substantiated in part: the request was raised once in writing and once, on the plant manager's own account, verbally, and neither was escalated. The third is not substantiated. The employee said she had been given that assurance; the plant manager said he had not given it; there is no record either way, and the investigation makes no finding on it. It is recommended that shift changes be communicated in writing, with acknowledgement, from the next cycle.

items.situation: Original: I was never told about the change. Report it.
tips: He said he had never been told about the change.
Said, not said me. And the verb goes back one step.

items.situation: Original: The deadline changed in May. She is the one who told you.
tips: She told me the deadline had changed in May.
Told needs the person straight after it.

items.situation: Original: What is the real deadline? Report the question.
tips: He asked what the real deadline was.

items.situation: Original: I will look into it and come back within a week.
tips: She said she would look into it and come back within a week.
Will becomes would. Would stays would.

items.situation: Somebody repeats what they heard in a corridor. Name it and say what you do with it.
tips: That is hearsay, so it is recorded but it is not in the findings.
Record it, label it, keep it out of the conclusions.

items.situation: One point cannot be proved. Say it in one sentence, without apologising.
tips: The third allegation is not substantiated, and the investigation makes no finding on it.
A note that substantiates everything is a note nobody believes.

listenings.text: There are three things people confuse, and confusing them is how a note becomes evidence against the company rather than for it. An allegation is what somebody claims. Hearsay is what somebody was told by a third person and did not witness. A finding is what you concluded and can support. Keep them in separate paragraphs and label them, because in eighteen months nobody will remember which was which and the document will be read by a lawyer, not by you. Second point. Report what was said, do not interpret it. He said he had not been told the deadline is a sentence I can defend. He clearly did not care about the deadline is a sentence that will cost us. And the last one, which people hate. If a point was not substantiated, write that it was not substantiated. A note that substantiates everything is a note nobody believes.

When I take one of these to the executive team, I have two minutes and three people who described the same afternoon differently. What I used to do was tell it chronologically, and by minute two nobody could hold three timelines in their head. What I do now is start with what is not in dispute. All three agree that the meeting happened on the fourteenth and that it lasted about forty minutes. That takes fifteen seconds and it steadies the room. Then I say where they diverge, in one sentence each. He said he had raised it twice. She said she had no record of either conversation. The third person told us she was not in the room. And then, only then, what I concluded and what I could not. If you start with the disagreement, everybody picks a side before they have the facts, and you spend the rest of the meeting arguing with people who chose in the first ten seconds.
